key_terms.meaning: A cyclic device that takes heat Q₁ from a hot reservoir, converts part into work W and rejects Q₂ to a cold reservoir.
A large body whose temperature stays fixed when heat enters or leaves it.
The source supplies heat at high temperature; the sink receives heat at low temperature.
For a heat engine, η = W/Q₁ = (Q₁ − Q₂)/Q₁.
Reversed heat engines that use work W to move heat from a cold region to a hot region.
COP<sub>R</sub> = Q₂/W for a refrigerator; COP<sub>HP</sub> = Q₁/W for a heat pump.
For the same two reservoirs and the same work input, the heat-pump COP is one more than the refrigerator COP.
A supposed cyclic machine that converts all heat from one reservoir into work; the second law forbids it.
No cyclic device can convert all heat from a single reservoir into work.
No cyclic device can transfer heat from a cold body to a hot body without external work.
A process that can be reversed so both system and surroundings return exactly to their initial states with no net change.
A process whose reverse would leave a permanent change in the system or surroundings.
A reversible cycle of two isothermal and two adiabatic processes between two reservoirs.
No engine between two fixed reservoirs can be more efficient than a reversible engine; all reversible engines have the same efficiency.
A scale defined by T₁/T₂ = Q₁/Q₂ for a reversible engine, independent of the working substance.
For any cycle, ∮δQ/T ≤ 0, with equality only for a reversible cycle.
A property S defined by dS = δQ<sub>rev</sub>/T for a reversible path; on the molecular scale S = k ln W counts arrangements.
For any process, ΔS<sub>total</sub> = ΔS<sub>system</sub> + ΔS<sub>surroundings</sub> ≥ 0, with equality only for a reversible process.
At absolute zero the entropy of a perfect crystal is zero, and absolute zero cannot be reached in a finite number of steps.
A refrigeration capacity unit equal to 3.517 kW of heat removal.
S₂ − S₁ = Σ Q/T + S<sub>gen</sub>; for steady flow, Ṡ<sub>gen</sub> = ṁ(s₂ − s₁) − Σ Q̇/T ≥ 0. Work carries no entropy.
W<sub>lost</sub> = T₀S<sub>gen</sub>, the work made unavailable by the entropy generated, with T₀ the surroundings temperature.
S = k ln W, with k = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K and W the number of microstates of one macrostate.

takeaways: The first law balances energy; the second law decides which energy transfers are possible and in which direction they occur.
A cyclic heat engine must reject some heat to a sink, so its thermal efficiency is always less than 100%.
COP can be greater than 1, and for the same reservoirs COP<sub>HP</sub> = COP<sub>R</sub> + 1.
The Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements are equivalent, and each forbids a different version of a perpetual-motion machine of the second kind.
Reversibility is an ideal limit; friction, finite temperature difference, unrestrained expansion and mixing create irreversibility.
Carnot efficiency η = 1 − T₂/T₁ is the upper bound for any engine working between T₁ and T₂ in kelvin; all reversible engines reach it.
Entropy is defined by dS = δQ<sub>rev</sub>/T; for an irreversible path, use a reversible path between the same end states to find ΔS.
The total entropy of system plus surroundings never decreases, and every real process generates entropy.
Entropy crosses a boundary only with heat and with mass; inside, irreversibility generates it. For steady flow, Ṡ<sub>gen</sub> = ṁ(s₂ − s₁) − Σ Q̇/T ≥ 0, and T₀Ṡ<sub>gen</sub> is the work lost.
On the molecular scale S = k ln W; the third law sets S = 0 for a perfect crystal at 0 K, and 0 K cannot be reached in a finite number of steps.
bank_note: Long answers usually stress the two second-law statements and their equivalence, the Carnot cycle and theorem, the Clausius inequality, entropy change in reversible and irreversible processes and the principle of increase of entropy. Some syllabi also ask for the microscopic interpretation of entropy and the entropy balance of a control volume.

bank.q: Define a heat engine, a refrigerator and a heat pump. Draw their energy-flow diagrams and show that COP<sub>HP</sub> = COP<sub>R</sub> + 1 when both work between the same two reservoirs.
outline: Define each device and label Q₁, Q₂ and W
Draw source, sink and work arrows for engine, refrigerator and heat pump
Use Q₁ = Q₂ + W from the first law for a cycle
Write COP<sub>R</sub> = Q₂/W and COP<sub>HP</sub> = Q₁/W
Substitute to get COP<sub>HP</sub> = COP<sub>R</sub> + 1, with a numerical check
answer: Common parts. A source (hot reservoir) at T₁, a sink (cold reservoir) at T₂ < T₁, and a device that works in a cycle between them. A thermal reservoir is a body so large that taking or adding heat does not change its temperature. Over one cycle the device returns to its starting state, so its internal energy change is zero and the first law reduces to a balance of heat and work: Q₁ = Q₂ + W, with all three taken as positive magnitudes.

Heat engine. A cyclic device that takes heat Q₁ from the source, converts part of it into net work W and rejects the rest, Q₂, to the sink. Its figure of merit is the thermal efficiency η = W/Q₁ = 1 − Q₂/Q₁, always below 1 because Q₂ > 0.

Refrigerator. The same kind of device run backwards: work W is supplied, heat Q₂ is removed from the cold space, and Q₁ = Q₂ + W is rejected to the warmer surroundings. The wanted effect is the cooling Q₂, so COPR = Q₂/W.
Heat pump. The same reversed cycle, but the wanted effect is the heat Q₁ delivered to the warm space (a room in winter, a water tank). So COPHP = Q₁/W.

answer.text: Energy-flow diagrams. The engine’s arrows run down from source to sink with work out; the refrigerator and heat pump have the same reversed arrows, and differ only in which heat is wanted.

answer.text: Derivation. For the reversed device the first law for a cycle gives Q₁ = Q₂ + W. Divide every term by W:

answer: Meaning. For the same machine, the same two reservoirs and the same work input, the heat pump always delivers exactly one unit of heat per unit of work more than the refrigerator removes, because the work itself also ends up as heat on the warm side.

answer.text: Numerical check. A machine takes W = 4 kW and removes Q₂ = 10 kW from a cold space.

answer: Why the two COPs behave differently. COPR can be below 1 when the temperature lift is large (a freezer in a hot room), because the work can exceed the heat removed. COPHP can never be below 1: even if the machine moved no heat at all, the work itself would arrive as heat, giving COPHP = 1.

Closing points. η is always below 1, but a COP is usually above 1: it compares heat moved with work paid, so it is not an efficiency and creates no energy. The relation holds for real and reversible machines alike, since it uses only the first law.

bank.q: State the Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements of the second law. Explain why each statement rules out a different impossible machine, and show that they are equivalent.
outline: State the Kelvin-Planck statement
Explain that it forbids a PMM2
State the Clausius statement
Explain that it forbids heat flow from cold to hot with no work input
Prove the equivalence: a violation of either gives a violation of the other
answer: Kelvin-Planck statement. It is impossible for any device that operates in a cycle to receive heat from a single reservoir and produce an equal amount of net work. Every heat engine must reject some heat to a colder body, so η = W/Q₁ < 1.

The machine it forbids. A perpetual motion machine of the second kind (PMM2): a cyclic engine with Q₂ = 0 and η = 100%, for example a ship running on the heat of the sea alone. A PMM2 would obey the first law (1000 kJ in, 1000 kJ of work out), so the first law cannot rule it out; this is the main limitation of the first law.
Clausius statement. It is impossible to construct a device that operates in a cycle and whose only effect is to transfer heat from a body at a lower temperature to a body at a higher temperature.

The machine it forbids. A work-free refrigerator: a sealed box that cools its inside and warms the room with no power supply. “Only effect” matters: a kitchen fridge moves heat from 4 °C to 35 °C, but it uses work from the socket, so it is allowed.

Different focus. Kelvin-Planck speaks about engines (heat into work); Clausius speaks about refrigerators (heat uphill). Both are postulates drawn from experience, and neither follows from the first law.

If Kelvin-Planck fails, Clausius fails. Let a PMM2 take Q from the hot body at T₁ and give W = Q. Use W to drive a reversible refrigerator that takes Q₂ from the cold body and gives Q₂ + W to the hot body. Net: the hot body gains (Q₂ + Q) − Q = Q₂, the cold body loses Q₂, and no outside work is used. Heat has gone uphill with no other effect.

If Clausius fails, Kelvin-Planck fails. Let a work-free device lift Q₂ from T₂ to T₁. Run an engine between the same bodies: it takes Q₁, gives W = Q₁ − Q₂ and rejects Q₂, which the device carries straight back. Net: the cold body is unchanged, the hot body loses Q₁ − Q₂, and the same amount appears as work. That is a PMM2.

answer.text: Numerical illustration (the chapter’s example, a reversible refrigerator of COP 1.5 between 500 K and 300 K driven by a 200 kJ PMM2):

answer: Conclusion. Each statement implies the other, so they are two forms of one law: the second law of thermodynamics.

bank.q: Define reversible and irreversible processes. List four causes of irreversibility, give one engineering example of each, and distinguish internal from external reversibility.
outline: Define a reversible process: no trace left in system or surroundings
State the two conditions: quasi-static and no dissipation
List friction, unrestrained expansion, heat transfer across a finite temperature difference and mixing, each with an example
Distinguish internal and external reversibility
Explain that all real processes are irreversible and why the reversible process is still useful
answer: Reversible process. A process after which the system and the surroundings can both be returned exactly to their initial states, leaving no change anywhere: no warmed oil, no worn bearing, no extra heat in the atmosphere.

Irreversible process. A process after which this full restoration is impossible: undoing it leaves a permanent change somewhere, usually work converted to internal energy or heat spread to a colder body.

Conditions for reversibility. (i) Quasi-static: the driving and resisting forces differ only infinitesimally (gas pressure p + dp against the piston, heat across T + dT), so the system passes through equilibrium states. (ii) No dissipative effects: no friction, viscosity, electrical resistance or plastic deformation. Both must hold; slowness alone is not enough.

answer.text: Causes of irreversibility with engineering examples.

head: cause
why it is irreversible
engineering example
rows: work becomes internal energy and never returns to the shaft by itself
piston rings rubbing in an engine cylinder; bearings of a pump
gas does no work as it spreads and will not gather back without work
a pressure vessel bursting; a throttle valve in a refrigerator
Heat transfer across a finite ΔT
heat will not flow back up the same temperature difference
flue gas at 1200 K heating water at 500 K in a boiler
Mixing of different fluids or states
feedwater heater mixing steam with water; hot and cold water in a shower line

answer: Further causes (also accepted): current through a resistance, plastic deformation, combustion and other fast chemical reactions, viscous flow through pipes.
Internal reversibility. No irreversibility inside the system boundary: no internal friction, no pressure or temperature gradients in the gas, so it is uniform at every instant.

External reversibility. No irreversibility at the boundary or in the surroundings: heat is exchanged only with a body at the same temperature, and work goes to a load with no outside friction. A totally reversible process is both internally and externally reversible; a gas compressed slowly in a frictionless cylinder while losing heat to a much colder room is internally reversible but externally irreversible.

answer.text: Why the ideal matters, with numbers: 0.5 kg of air at 300 K going from 0.2 m³ to 0.4 m³.
answer.pre:
reversible isothermal:  W = mRT ln(V₂/V₁) = 43.05 × 0.6931 = 29.84 kJ
free expansion:         W = 0
work lost:              29.84 kJ

answer: Conclusion. Every real process is irreversible. The reversible process gives the maximum work from an expansion and the minimum work for a compression, so it is the yardstick; the gap from a real device is the lost work, measured by the entropy generated.

bank.q: Describe the Carnot cycle with p-V and T-s diagrams. Derive η<sub>Carnot</sub> = 1 − T₂/T₁ for an ideal gas.
outline: Name the two isothermal and two adiabatic processes
Draw p-V and T-s diagrams with heat transfer directions
Write Q₁ at T₁ and Q₂ at T₂
Link the volumes through the two adiabats
Derive efficiency as 1 − T₂/T₁ and check with numbers
answer: The cycle. m kg of ideal gas in a frictionless piston-cylinder works between a source at T₁ and a sink at T₂. All four processes are reversible: 1→2 isothermal expansion at T₁ (heat Q₁ in, work out); 2→3 reversible adiabatic expansion (T falls from T₁ to T₂, work out); 3→4 isothermal compression at T₂ (heat Q₂ out, work in); 4→1 reversible adiabatic compression (T rises from T₂ to T₁, work in).

answer.text: Diagrams. On p-V axes: two falling isotherms (pV constant) joined by two steeper adiabats (pVγ constant); the enclosed area is the net work. On T-s axes: a rectangle, the isotherms horizontal at T₁ and T₂ and the reversible adiabats vertical; the area under 1→2 is Q₁, under 3→4 is Q₂, and the rectangle itself is W.

answer.text: Heat in the isothermal steps. For an ideal gas at constant T, ΔU = 0, so Q = W = mRT ln(Vfinal/Vinitial):
answer.pre:
Q₁ = mRT₁ ln(V₂/V₁)          (taken in, 1→2)
Q₂ = mRT₂ ln(V₃/V₄)          (rejected, 3→4, as a positive magnitude)

answer.text: The adiabats link the volumes. For a reversible adiabatic process of an ideal gas, TVγ−1 is constant:
answer.pre:
2→3:  T₁V₂<sup>γ−1</sup> = T₂V₃<sup>γ−1</sup>
4→1:  T₁V₁<sup>γ−1</sup> = T₂V₄<sup>γ−1</sup>
divide:  (V₂/V₁)<sup>γ−1</sup> = (V₃/V₄)<sup>γ−1</sup>   so   V₂/V₁ = V₃/V₄

answer.text: Efficiency. The two logarithms are equal and cancel:
answer.pre:
η = W/Q₁ = (Q₁ − Q₂)/Q₁ = 1 − Q₂/Q₁
  = 1 − [mRT₂ ln(V₃/V₄)] / [mRT₁ ln(V₂/V₁)]
  = 1 − T₂/T₁

answer: What the result says. η depends only on the two reservoir temperatures in kelvin, not on the gas, the mass or the pressures. Raising T₁ or lowering T₂ raises it; it reaches 1 only if T₂ = 0 K, which the third law forbids.

answer: Closing point. The Carnot cycle is the most efficient cycle between two fixed temperatures, but it is impractical on a gas: in the example the volume grows about 31 times for only 119.4 kJ of work, and slow isothermal heat transfer would need huge equipment.

bank.q: Explain the microscopic interpretation of entropy. Use Boltzmann’s relation to find the entropy change when 1 kg of nitrogen (R = 0.2968 kJ/(kg·K), molar mass 28.013 kg/kmol) doubles its volume at constant temperature, and check the answer with the macroscopic formula.
outline: Distinguish macrostate and microstate
State S = k ln W with symbols and units
Explain why more arrangements means more entropy, and why heat (not work) carries entropy
Count microstates for a doubling of volume: W rises by 2ᴺ
Compute N, Nk and ΔS, and check against mR ln(V₂/V₁)
answer: Two levels of description. A macrostate is the state we measure: p, V, T, the mass. A microstate is one exact arrangement of every molecule’s position and energy. A huge number of microstates W give the same macrostate, because swapping or shifting molecules does not change the measured p, V and T.

Boltzmann’s relation. S = k ln W, where k = 1.381 × 10−23 J/K is Boltzmann’s constant (the universal gas constant per molecule, R̄/NA) and W is the number of microstates. Entropy is a measure of the number of ways the molecules can be arranged consistent with what we measure.

Why it matches thermodynamics. A system left alone moves to the macrostate with the most microstates, simply because that macrostate is overwhelmingly the most probable; this is the increase of entropy. Heat added to a body opens more energy arrangements, and the same heat added at a lower temperature opens relatively more, which is why dS = δQrev/T. Work moves molecules together in an ordered way and opens no new arrangements, so work carries no entropy.

Counting for a doubling of volume. At constant temperature the energy arrangements do not change; only the room for each molecule doubles. Each molecule has twice as many places to be, so with N molecules W₂ = 2NW₁.

answer.text: Entropy change from Boltzmann.
answer.pre: ΔS = k ln W₂ − k ln W₁ = k ln(W₂/W₁) = k ln 2<sup>N</sup> = Nk ln 2

answer.text: Numbers for 1 kg of nitrogen.
Macroscopic check. For an ideal gas at constant temperature, ΔS = mR ln(V₂/V₁):

answer: Why they agree. Nk = (m/M) NA × R̄/NA = mR̄/M = mR. The two results, 0.2058 and 0.2057 kJ/K, differ only in the fourth figure, from rounding the constants. The molecular count and the heat-over-temperature definition are the same entropy.

Closing points. The entropy rises because the gas has more ways to be arranged, even though no heat need enter (in a free expansion Q = 0 and ΔS is the same 0.2057 kJ/K, all of it generated). A perfect crystal at 0 K has one arrangement, W = 1, so S = k ln 1 = 0: the third law. Calling entropy “disorder” is a loose summary of this counting.

bank.q: A Carnot engine receives 900 kJ/min from a reservoir at 750 K and rejects heat at 300 K. Find its efficiency, work output per minute (and power in kW) and heat rejected per minute. Check the result with the Clausius inequality.
outline: Use η = 1 − T₂/T₁ with kelvin temperatures
W = ηQ₁ = 540 kJ/min = 9 kW
Q₂ = Q₁ − W = 360 kJ/min
Check: Q₁/T₁ − Q₂/T₂ = 0 for a reversible engine
answer: Data. Q₁ = 900 kJ/min, T₁ = 750 K, T₂ = 300 K. The engine is a Carnot engine, so it is reversible.
Assumptions. The engine is reversible (a Carnot engine), the reservoirs stay at fixed temperatures, and the rates are steady, so “per minute” quantities can be treated like quantities per cycle.

answer: The extra work, 0.949 kW, equals T₁ times the entropy generated: every bit of entropy the real machine generates must be paid for in compressor work.

Same machine as a heat pump. If the 5.429 kW rejected were the wanted output (heating a room at 35 °C from the 2 °C side):

Comment. The real refrigerator reaches about a third of the Carnot COP. The Carnot COP shows that the temperature lift of 33 K, not the hardware, limits any refrigerator to at most 8.33.

bank.q: One kg of air expands reversibly and isothermally at 400 K from 3 bar to 1 bar. Take R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K). Find the entropy change of the air, the heat absorbed and the work done, and show the process on a T-s diagram.

q = TΔs = 126.1 kJ/kg for a reversible isothermal process
ΔU = 0, so w = q = 126.1 kJ/kg
T-s diagram: a horizontal line at 400 K, area under it = heat
answer: Data. m = 1 kg, T = 400 K constant, p₁ = 3 bar, p₂ = 1 bar, R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K). The process is reversible, so the area under the T-s path is the heat.

Assumptions. Air is an ideal gas with constant R; the expansion is reversible (quasi-static, no friction) and the temperature stays at 400 K because heat flows in from a source at 400 K as the gas does work; kinetic and potential energy changes are negligible.

answer.text: Entropy change. From ds = cp dT/T − R dp/p with dT = 0:

answer: The entropy rises: heat flows in to keep the temperature constant as the gas expands.

answer.text: Heat absorbed. For a reversible process at constant T, Q = TΔS:
Work done. For an ideal gas at constant temperature Δu = 0, so by the first law w = q. Check with the work formula:
T-s diagram. The process is a horizontal line at 400 K, 0.3153 kJ/(kg·K) long; the shaded area under it is the 126.1 kJ/kg of heat.

Same end states, irreversible path. Suppose the air reached 1 bar and 400 K by expanding freely into a vacuum instead. Entropy is a property, so Δs is the same, but no heat enters:
answer.pre:
Δs = 0.3153 kJ/(kg·K),   q = 0,   w = 0
s<sub>gen</sub> = Δs − q/T = 0.3153 kJ/(kg·K)
lost work (surroundings at 300 K) = 300 × 0.3153 = 94.6 kJ/kg

answer: This is why the area under a T-s path equals heat only for a reversible path: the free expansion has the same end points and the same Δs, but zero heat.
Closing check. If the source supplying the heat is also at 400 K, its entropy falls by 126.1/400 = 0.3153 kJ/K and the total change is zero, as it must be for a totally reversible process.

bank.q: A cyclic device receives 800 kJ at 500 K, rejects 500 kJ at 300 K and produces 300 kJ of work. Test it with the first law and the Clausius inequality; state whether it is reversible, irreversible or impossible.
outline: Check the first law: 800 − 500 = 300 kJ
Evaluate ∮δQ/T = 800/500 − 500/300 with signs
Get −0.067 kJ/K, less than zero
A negative value means irreversible but possible
Confirm with η against the Carnot efficiency and find the entropy generated
answer: Sign convention. Heat into the device is positive, heat out negative. Q₁ = +800 kJ at T₁ = 500 K, Q₂ = −500 kJ at T₂ = 300 K, W = 300 kJ.

answer.text: First law for a cycle.

answer: The energy balance closes, so the first law alone cannot reject the device.

answer.text: Clausius inequality.

answer: The cyclic integral is −0.0667 kJ/K, which is less than zero. The Clausius inequality ∮δQ/T ≤ 0 is satisfied, with strict inequality.
Verdict. The device is possible but irreversible. (Zero would mean reversible; a positive value would mean impossible.)

answer.text: Check with efficiencies.
answer.pre:
η = W/Q₁ = 300/800 = 0.375
η<sub>Carnot</sub> = 1 − 300/500 = 0.40
0.375 < 0.40, so the device is real but below the reversible limit

answer.text: Entropy generated and lost work. The working fluid returns to its state, so the generation shows up in the reservoirs:
answer.pre:
S<sub>gen</sub> = −∮δQ/T = 0.0667 kJ/K per cycle
reversible work from 800 kJ = 0.40 × 800 = 320 kJ
lost work = 320 − 300 = 20 kJ = T₂ S<sub>gen</sub> = 300 × 0.0667 = 20 kJ

answer.text: Where the boundaries lie. Keep Q₁ = 800 kJ at 500 K and vary the heat rejected at 300 K:

answer: The reversible case rejects Q₁T₂/T₁ = 800 × 300/500 = 480 kJ. Any device that rejects less than 480 kJ while taking 800 kJ at 500 K would beat the Carnot efficiency and would give a positive integral; the test catches it in one line.

Sign check. Entering the rejected heat as +500 kJ would give 1.6 + 1.667 = +3.27 kJ/K and the device would be wrongly called impossible. Heat leaving the system always enters the integral with a minus sign.
Conclusion. Irreversible: it obeys both laws, generates 0.0667 kJ/K of entropy per cycle and loses 20 kJ of work compared with a reversible engine between the same reservoirs.

Take c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 kJ/(kg·K), R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K) and T₀ = 300 K, and neglect kinetic and potential energy. Find the power, the rate of entropy generation, the lost work and the isentropic efficiency.

Entropy change of the air from the ideal-gas formula
Adiabatic steady flow: Ṡ<sub>gen</sub> = ṁ(s₂ − s₁)
Lost work T₀Ṡ<sub>gen</sub>
Isentropic exit temperature and isentropic efficiency
answer: Data. ṁ = 2 kg/s; inlet p₁ = 800 kPa, T₁ = 900 K; exit p₂ = 100 kPa, T₂ = 540 K; insulated, so Q̇ = 0; T₀ = 300 K.

Assumptions. Steady flow; air is an ideal gas with constant cp; the casing is insulated, so no heat crosses and the only entropy transfer is with the stream; kinetic and potential energy changes are negligible; the surroundings, used for the lost work, are at T₀ = 300 K.

answer.text: Power, from the steady flow energy equation with Q̇ = 0 and no kinetic or potential energy change:
Entropy change of the air.
Entropy generation. Steady flow, one inlet and one exit, no heat:

answer: Ṡ<sub>gen</sub> is positive, so the turbine is possible and irreversible (fluid friction in the blade passages is the main source).

answer.text: Lost work.
Isentropic turbine between the same pressures (s₂ₛ = s₁):
Isentropic efficiency.
Summary.

answer: T-s picture. State 1 is at 900 K on the 800 kPa line. The isentropic expansion drops vertically to 2s at 497.0 K on the 100 kPa line; the real expansion ends further right and higher, at 540 K, because s rises by 0.0834 kJ/(kg·K). The horizontal gap between 2s and 2 is the entropy generated per kg.

Closing check. The isentropic power exceeds the actual power by 810.1 − 723.6 = 86.5 kW, more than the 50.1 kW of lost work. The difference is not a mistake: the actual exhaust leaves hotter (540 K against 497 K) and still carries some energy that could do work, so only 50.1 kW is truly destroyed.

bank.q: Prove Carnot’s theorem: no engine between two reservoirs is more efficient than a reversible engine, and all reversible engines between the same two reservoirs have the same efficiency.
outline: Assume an engine X more efficient than a reversible engine R
Give both the same Q₁ and run R backwards on part of X’s work
The hot reservoir is unchanged; the surplus work comes from the cold reservoir alone
This is a PMM2, violating Kelvin-Planck
Repeat with two reversible engines both ways to prove equality; state the consequences
answer: Statement. (1) No heat engine working between two given reservoirs can be more efficient than a reversible engine working between the same reservoirs. (2) All reversible engines working between the same two reservoirs have the same efficiency, whatever their working substance.

Set-up for part 1. Let R be a reversible engine and X any engine, both between a hot reservoir at T₁ and a cold reservoir at T₂. Suppose, against the theorem, ηX > ηR. Let both take the same heat Q₁ from the hot reservoir. Then WX = ηXQ₁ > WR = ηRQ₁, and X rejects less heat: Q₁ − WX < Q₁ − WR.

Reverse R. Because R is reversible, it can run as a refrigerator with every quantity the same size and reversed: driven by WR, it takes Q₁ − WR from the cold reservoir and delivers Q₁ to the hot reservoir. Drive it with part of X’s work.

answer.text: Net effect of X plus reversed R (with numbers for ηX = 0.5, ηR = 0.4, Q₁ = 100 kJ):

answer: Contradiction. The combination works in a cycle, exchanges heat with the cold reservoir only, and turns that heat completely into work. That is a perpetual motion machine of the second kind, which the Kelvin-Planck statement forbids. So ηX > ηR is impossible: ηX ≤ ηR.

Part 2. Let A and B be two reversible engines between the same reservoirs. Applying part 1 with X = A and R = B gives ηA ≤ ηB. Both are reversible, so the roles can be swapped: X = B and R = A gives ηB ≤ ηA. Hence ηA = ηB.

Note on the proof. Only the reversible engine is reversed. An irreversible engine cannot run backwards with the same heats and work, which is why the argument proves “≤” for any engine but “=” only between reversible ones.

Consequences. (i) The reversible efficiency depends only on the two reservoir temperatures; this is what allows the thermodynamic temperature scale, T₁/T₂ = Q₁/Q₂, and gives ηrev = 1 − T₂/T₁. (ii) Any claim above 1 − T₂/T₁ can be rejected at once. (iii) The working fluid, size and pressures of a reversible engine do not matter, so a Carnot cycle on an ideal gas gives the result for every substance.
Check. Between 900 K and 300 K every reversible engine gives η = 1 − 300/900 = 0.667; an air Carnot cycle with V₂/V₁ = 2 gives Q₁ = 179.0 kJ and W = 119.4 kJ, the same 0.667.

bank.q: A firm claims an engine with efficiency 45% working between 600 K and 320 K. Evaluate the claim using Carnot’s theorem and entropy.
outline: Carnot efficiency = 1 − 320/600 = 46.7%
Compare the claimed 45% with 46.7%
Below the limit: not forbidden by the second law
Entropy generation per 100 kJ is positive (0.0052 kJ/K)
Lost work equals the gap from the reversible engine; judge how realistic the claim is
answer: Data. T₁ = 600 K, T₂ = 320 K, claimed η = 0.45. Take a basis of Q₁ = 100 kJ from the source.

Assumptions. The engine works in a cycle between two reservoirs of fixed temperature, the stated efficiency is the cycle efficiency W/Q₁, and the working fluid returns to its initial state each cycle, so its own entropy change is zero.

answer.text: Carnot limit.

answer: Comparison. 45% < 46.7%, so by Carnot’s theorem the claim is not impossible. It is below the reversible limit, so the engine must be irreversible, but only slightly.

answer.text: Energy flows on the 100 kJ basis.
answer.pre:
W = 0.45 × 100 = 45 kJ
Q₂ = 100 − 45 = 55 kJ   rejected at 320 K

answer.text: Entropy test. Over one cycle the working fluid returns to its state, so only the reservoirs change:

answer: S<sub>gen</sub> is positive, so the second law is satisfied; the Clausius integral is 100/600 − 55/320 = −0.00521 kJ/K < 0, telling the same story.

answer.text: Lost work. Against a reversible engine between the same reservoirs:
answer.pre:
W<sub>rev</sub> = 0.4667 × 100 = 46.67 kJ
W<sub>rev</sub> − W = 46.67 − 45 = 1.67 kJ
T₂ S<sub>gen</sub> = 320 × 0.00521 = 1.67 kJ   (agrees)

answer.text: Reversible reference for comparison.
Where the line falls. The same entropy test rejects a claim of 48%:
Sensitivity to the sink temperature. If the heat were in fact rejected at 330 K, the limit itself would be 45%:
answer.pre:
η<sub>Carnot</sub> = 1 − 330/600 = 0.45
the claim would then need a perfectly reversible engine: not credible

answer: Evaluation. Thermodynamically the claim is allowed. Practically it is very doubtful: the engine would have to reach 45/46.7 = 96% of the Carnot efficiency, with almost no friction and almost no temperature difference in its heat exchangers. Real engines between these temperatures reach well under 80% of Carnot. The firm should be asked for test data. If the claim had been above 46.7%, Sgen would come out negative and it could be rejected outright.

bank.q: Derive the Clausius inequality using a cycle coupled to reversible engines and a single reservoir. Use it to show that entropy is a property, and explain why ∮δQ/T < 0 for an irreversible cycle.
outline: Couple each heat transfer δQ at boundary temperature T to a reversible engine fed from one reservoir at T₀
Total heat from T₀ is T₀∮δQ/T, and it all becomes work
Kelvin-Planck forbids positive work, so ∮δQ/T ≤ 0
Equality for a reversible cycle: two reversible paths give the same ∫δQ/T, so S is a property
Irreversible cycle: reversing it would give a positive integral, so the strict inequality holds; link to S<sub>gen</sub>
answer: Set-up. A system undergoes any cycle. Wherever a small heat δQ crosses its boundary, the boundary temperature is T (in kelvin). Sign: δQ positive into the system.

Reference engines. At each such place put a small reversible engine between a single large reservoir at T₀ and the boundary at T. It supplies exactly the δQ the system receives there. Being reversible, its heats are in the ratio of temperatures (thermodynamic scale), so it draws δQ₀ = δQ T₀/T from the reservoir and delivers work δWe = δQ₀ − δQ.

answer.text: The combined device (system plus all small engines) works in a cycle and exchanges heat with the single reservoir at T₀ only:
answer.pre:
heat from T₀ in one cycle:   Q₀ = ∮ δQ T₀/T = T₀ ∮ δQ/T
first law for the cycle:      W<sub>total</sub> = Q₀ = T₀ ∮ δQ/T

answer: Apply Kelvin-Planck. A cyclic device that exchanges heat with one reservoir cannot deliver positive net work. So Wtotal ≤ 0. Since T₀ > 0, this gives the Clausius inequality:

Reversible cycle: equality. If the cycle is reversible, run it backwards: every δQ changes sign, so the integral changes sign, and the backward cycle must also give ≤ 0. Both ≤ 0 and ≥ 0 hold, so ∮δQ/T = 0 for a reversible cycle.

answer.text: Entropy is a property. Take two reversible paths A and B from state 1 to state 2. Go 1→2 along A and back 2→1 along B reversed; this is a reversible cycle:

answer: The integral of δQ<sub>rev</sub>/T between two states is the same for every reversible path, so it depends only on the end states. It defines a property: dS = δQ<sub>rev</sub>/T.

Irreversible cycle: strict inequality. If ∮δQ/T were zero for an irreversible cycle, the combined device would deliver zero net work and leave no change in the reservoir; the cycle and the small reversible engines could then be undone with no trace, which contradicts the irreversibility. So ∮δQ/T < 0. Physically, irreversibility generates entropy inside; to return to its start each cycle the system must reject that extra entropy as heat, which makes the negative terms larger: ∮δQ/T = −Sgen.

answer.text: Numerical illustration.

answer: Conclusion. ∮δQ/T ≤ 0 for every cycle: zero for reversible cycles (which makes entropy a property) and negative for irreversible ones, the amount being the entropy generated per cycle.

bank.q: Discuss the third law of thermodynamics, absolute entropy, and the unattainability of absolute zero. Explain why reaching 0 K would need an infinite number of steps, and find the absolute entropy at 10 K of a solid with c<sub>p</sub> = 0.002T³ J/(mol·K).
outline: Nernst heat theorem and Planck’s statement: S = 0 for a perfect crystal at 0 K
Absolute entropy by integrating c<sub>p</sub>/T from 0 K, plus phase-change terms
Debye law: S = aT³/3, worked to 0.667 J/(mol·K) at 10 K
Unattainability: entropy curves meet at 0 K, so the step size shrinks
Residual entropy of glasses; consequences such as c<sub>p</sub> → 0
answer: Nernst heat theorem. For a condensed system in equilibrium, the entropy change of any isothermal process tends to zero as T → 0 K.

Third law (Planck’s form). The entropy of a perfect crystal in equilibrium is zero at absolute zero. On the molecular scale a perfect crystal at 0 K has a single arrangement, W = 1, so S = k ln 1 = 0.

Absolute entropy. With a fixed zero, entropy at any temperature is an absolute value, found by heating the substance reversibly from 0 K: S(T) = ∫ cp dT/T from 0 to T, plus ΔHtr/Ttr for every melting, boiling or crystal change on the way. Chemical data tables list such absolute (standard) entropies. (Steam tables, by contrast, use an arbitrary zero at the triple point, which is enough for changes.)

answer.text: Worked value at 10 K. With cp = aT³, a = 0.002 J/(mol·K⁴), and S(0) = 0:
The integral converges only because c<sub>p</sub> → 0. With a constant c<sub>p</sub> equal to its 10 K value, 2 J/(mol·K), the classical formula would give values that fall without limit:

answer: Consequence for heat capacity. Because S(0) is finite, cp/T must stay finite as T → 0, so cp and cv must tend to zero. Treating them as constant near 0 K gives a negative, diverging entropy.

Unattainability of absolute zero. Low temperatures are reached by repeated isothermal and adiabatic steps, for example adiabatic demagnetisation of a magnetic salt: magnetise it at constant T (heat flows out, S falls), then isolate it and remove the field (T falls). On a T-S diagram the curves for field on and field off are drawn closer together as T falls and meet at 0 K, as the Nernst theorem demands. Each step therefore gives a smaller temperature drop than the one before, and an infinite number of steps would be needed to reach 0 K.
Statement. No finite sequence of processes can bring a system to absolute zero. Laboratories reach microkelvin or nanokelvin temperatures, but never exactly 0 K.

Limits of the law. It applies to perfect crystals in equilibrium. Glasses, solid solutions and crystals with frozen-in disorder keep a residual entropy at 0 K, because more than one arrangement remains.

Evaluation. The third law adds no new limit to engine efficiency, but it completes the second: it fixes the zero of entropy, explains why cp → 0, and shows why the sink temperature in η = 1 − T₂/T₁ can never be 0 K, so no engine reaches 100%.

bank.q: Compare the Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements. Explain PMM2, and show with numbers how entropy generation measures irreversibility in real devices.
outline: State both statements and how each forbids a different machine
Equivalence by contradiction
PMM2: obeys the first law, breaks the second
Define entropy generation from ΔS<sub>total</sub> and from the control-volume balance
Numerical cases: heat across a finite ΔT, mixing of water, an air compressor, each with lost work T₀S<sub>gen</sub>
answer: Kelvin-Planck. No device operating in a cycle can receive heat from a single reservoir and produce net work. Clausius. No device operating in a cycle can have as its only effect the transfer of heat from a colder to a hotter body.

answer.text: Comparison.

head: Kelvin-Planck
Clausius
rows: every power plant has a condenser or radiator

answer: Equivalence. If a PMM2 existed, its work could drive a reversible refrigerator, and the pair would move heat from cold to hot with no outside work: Clausius would fail. If a work-free refrigerator existed, it could return an engine’s rejected heat to the source, and the pair would turn heat from one reservoir entirely into work: Kelvin-Planck would fail. So the two statements stand or fall together.

PMM2. A perpetual motion machine of the second kind is a cyclic engine that converts all the heat it takes from one reservoir into work. It obeys the first law (energy in = energy out) but breaks the second. A PMM1, by contrast, creates work from nothing and breaks the first law.

answer.text: Entropy generation. For any process, the entropy of everything involved obeys
answer.pre:
S<sub>gen</sub> = ΔS<sub>system</sub> + ΔS<sub>surroundings</sub> ≥ 0
steady flow:  Ṡ<sub>gen</sub> = ṁ(s₂ − s₁) − Σ Q̇/T ≥ 0
lost work:    W<sub>lost</sub> = T₀ S<sub>gen</sub>

answer: S<sub>gen</sub> is zero only for a reversible process and grows with the degree of irreversibility; a negative S<sub>gen</sub> means the process is impossible. A PMM2 would take entropy Q/T from its reservoir and put none anywhere else, giving S<sub>gen</sub> = −Q/T < 0, which is why the entropy statement contains both earlier statements.

answer.text: Case 1: heat across a finite temperature difference. 100 kJ flows from a body at 500 K to one at 300 K (surroundings at 300 K):
answer.pre:
S<sub>gen</sub> = 100/300 − 100/500 = 0.3333 − 0.2000 = 0.1333 kJ/K
W<sub>lost</sub> = 300 × 0.1333 = 40 kJ = 100 × (1 − 300/500), the work a reversible engine would have given

answer: Evaluation. The two statements tell us that some machines are impossible; entropy generation tells us how far a possible machine is from the ideal, in one number with units. Multiplied by T₀ it becomes lost work in kJ or kW, so an engineer can add the losses of a whole plant and fix the largest first. That is why the entropy form is the one used in design, while the two statements remain the clearest way to state the law.

glossary.def: A body large enough that its temperature remains constant when heat is added or removed.
A thermal reservoir at high temperature that supplies heat to a device.
A thermal reservoir at low temperature that receives rejected heat.
A cyclic device that converts part of the heat taken from a source into work.
The ratio of work output to heat input of a heat engine, η = W/Q₁.
A device that uses work to remove heat from a cold region and reject it to a warmer region.
The ratio of useful heat transfer to work input for a refrigerator or heat pump.
A reversed heat engine used to deliver heat to a warm space.
A refrigeration capacity equal to 3.517 kW of heat removal.
A perpetual-motion machine of the second kind, which would convert all heat from one reservoir into work in a cycle.
No cyclic device can produce work by exchanging heat with only one reservoir.
Heat cannot move from a cold body to a hot body in a cycle without work input.
An ideal process that can be reversed without leaving any net change in system or surroundings.
A real process that leaves a permanent change and cannot be fully reversed.
A process with no irreversibility inside the system boundary; any irreversibility lies in the surroundings.
The reversible cycle made of two isothermal and two adiabatic processes between two reservoirs.
No engine between two fixed reservoirs can be more efficient than a reversible engine.
A temperature scale based on reversible heat transfers, T₁/T₂ = Q₁/Q₂.
For any cycle, ∮δQ/T ≤ 0, with equality only for a reversible cycle.
A thermodynamic property whose change for a reversible path is dS = δQ<sub>rev</sub>/T.
The extra entropy created by irreversibilities within a process.
A plot of temperature against entropy used to show heat transfer and cycle performance.
The total entropy of an isolated system never decreases.
The entropy of a perfect crystal is zero at absolute zero.
Entropy measured from the zero set by the third law at 0 K.
Absolute zero cannot be reached in a finite number of cooling steps.
Change of entropy = entropy carried in by heat and mass − entropy carried out + entropy generated.
One exact arrangement of the molecules’ positions and energies; many microstates make one measured macrostate.
The work made unavailable by irreversibility, T₀ times the entropy generated.
